title: Morton's pride, the Decca date and the visit to his Washington club
summary: Morton refused a sideman role on Louis Armstrong's Decca date; Russell describes the room on U Street.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Remembering Jelly Roll Morton: the man, the band

blocks.x: He received you very ambly, though.

Yeah, very friendly. When Jelly, you see, there was that seniority business, too, that he wouldn't have, Judy, being younger, wouldn't have dared be leader. Once they wanted Jelly to record with Victor, I mean, with Decca, with Louis Armstrong, is what I'm trying to say, when they made that new Arlene's album that Louis made, and Steve Smith also organized that date. The same one that Judy was in, had a band, and the one where they makes the 219 blues. Sidney Bechet was on the date, too. And Jelly was supposed to be on that date, too. They wanted to line it up, you know, just like all of us make a lot of dumb mistakes and pick bands that maybe, with musicians that aren't necessarily suitable to play together, and the other, although certainly Jelly would have enjoyed playing with Louis and Sidney Bechet, and had wanted to, and his heart was sort of broken, that he couldn't. But he wouldn't do it, though, unless he could have been the leader. He would have a young kid about half his age, like Louis wasn't half his age, but consider when Jelly was somebody, Louis was a little kid, you know, in the home, maybe. And the same way with Sidney, although Sidney amounted to more at that time than Louis did, say in that 1910 period or so, or 15 period. Yet Jelly wouldn't have played as a side man with them. He was proud. I mean, he was, and figured he should have been the leader. And at least should have gotten paid as much as the other guys, as Louis say. But naturally, Decca at that time, I think, had Louis under contract, exclusive contract, and he, Louis was the leader of his band, and that's all there was to it. I know Charles Smith said it's sort of pitiful that Jelly was in the next, when they were rehearsing, Jelly happened to be in another, probably the NOLA studio or someplace, in one room rehearsing, and I heard the other band was in the, the whole New Orleans band was in the next room rehearsing, and Jelly was hoping he could be with him, but he couldn't. So they wouldn't pay Jelly anymore. They told Jelly he'd pay him a scale, and he was a side man, and that was it. Take it or leave it. And Jelly, of course, didn't have to take that, he'd starve before he'd take that kind of talk, so he wasn't on the date. So he was very proud, and in some cases, maybe hard to get along with too, but none of the greatest musicians I ever talked to, let me say the Dodds or Simeon or any of those that worked with him, Mitchell, oh no, Jelly is fine. No, I didn't have any trouble. No, I never heard he was hard to get along with. Mitchell will say, no. He maybe rehearsed and made him play certain things the way Jelly wanted him, but that was all. But anyway, this, I'll mention, I'll read a little bit of this. It was about, the winter of, spring of 1938 was one time, and another time, the winter of probably 37, that I first went to Sime. One time, I remember, I was with this Red Gate Shadow Players, and we, this one, Roosevelt at least, well, he was in the White House so long it could be any time, before 1944. Jelly was dead before he went. But I know one time, I was late setting up the stage. They were mad because I was out looking for records or else went to see Jelly. I forget what it was at the White House. I was much more interested in Jelly, of course, than the White House. But it was easy enough to find as long as you had the address there on U Street. I have here a note, the room is rather large but narrow. And as Charles Smith had told me, it was too brightly lit for a nightclub, mostly just a lot of high ceiling lamps. And he had only a little new spinet, quite a small piano against one wall and a jukebox back towards the kitchen. I drew a plan of it here. It was about, seven or eight tables maybe in the place. And when I told him, as I say, that I had all those old records like the Pearls and Wolverine while he hurried into the kitchen.
Which place is that now? Music Box. The same place here.
